docs.title: Giving ordinary motors a sense of position.
docs.text:
Elijah Koiki's motor encoder subsystem for the 2 DOF Smart Robot Arm Joint Showcase. Four optical channels turn the motion of two DC motor shafts into position and direction feedback for a distributed embedded control system.

Explore the schematic → Follow the signal path

docs.title: Project summary
docs.text:
Team 103 is developing a modular, computer-connected control system for a two-degree-of-freedom robotic arm. Custom PCBs add sensing, communication and motor control to basic DC motors rated no higher than 12 V. My board measures both shafts using optical quadrature encoders, conditions their signals, and uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to prepare feedback for the main controller. This feedback is intended to support the team's closed-loop motion control and telemetry. See the Team 103 report for the wider system.

2Motor shafts monitored4Optical A/B channels5 VLocal logic supplyRev BERC-reviewed schematic

docs.title: My contribution
docs.text: I am responsible for the motor encoder subsystem: shaft sensing, analog filtering and amplification, digital edge conditioning, local power regulation, and the encoder PIC's connection to the main board. Connor's main board receives the proposed feedback link; Walker's motor driver board controls motor power. Encoder firmware and physical integration are the next implementation steps.

docs.title: Signal path and design decisions
docs.text:
Stage Function Design rationale Shafts and disks One patterned disk per motor; two sensors per disk A/B phase order supplies direction as well as incremental motion. Four TCST2103 sensors LED and phototransistor channels E1A, E1B, E2A, E2B Bare optical components expose the analog signal for a custom front end. RC + MCP6004 4.7 kΩ pull-up / 1 nF node filtering; nominal non-inverting gain 1.5 Repeated channels support matched conditioning; gain and bandwidth need bench confirmation. SN74HC14 Four Schmitt inverter gates Hysteresis converts slow analog transitions into digital edges. Both A/B channels are inverted, preserving their relative quadrature sequence. PIC18F57Q43 Nano RB0–RB3 receive A/B signals; proposed interrupt-driven decoding Counts and timing can provide relative position and speed. Team connection Proposed RC6 TX / RC7 RX through J6, with TX isolation jumper JP1 A local serial feedback link reduces the number of signals the main board must process. Final bus allocation is pending.

The encoder board measures motion; Walker's board supplies motor actuation. Separating these roles allows the team to inspect encoder performance independently of the driver. Connor's main controller is the proposed recipient of the feedback and the connection to the PC.

docs.title: Power and interface boundaries
docs.text:
J1 accepts the schematic's 9–12 V center-positive DC input. F1 and U1 provide a fused input and regulated +5 V for the Nano, sensors and conditioning circuits. The team PRD uses 9 V; 12 V is a schematic allowance that increases heating and requires thermal verification. The ribbon shares ground, not the local regulated power rail.

J2–J5 each use three cable conductors: LED drive, phototransistor collector signal, and common ground. The bare sensor has four physical leads; its LED cathode and transistor emitter share the cable ground. Physical sensor lead markings must be checked against the datasheet.

docs.title: Position, speed and mounting
docs.text:
For a disk with N slots, a quadrature decoder counting all four edges yields 4N counts per disk revolution. Per-channel pulse frequency is N × shaft RPM / 60; speed can be estimated from count change over a known time interval. Gear ratio must be included if a motor-shaft encoder is used to report joint angle.

Mount each A/B pair 90 electrical degrees apart. The corresponding mechanical offset is 90° / N, modulo the slot pitch. Shaft diameter, disk radius, slot count, maximum RPM and bracket clearances remain dependent on the selected motors. These incremental encoders also need a defined home/reference procedure after power-up.

docs.title: Optical sensing — individual subsystem
docs.text:
Candidate Advantages for this project Limitations Decision Vishay TCST2103 Bare transmissive LED/phototransistor; analog collector node accessible to the custom front end Needs a slotted disk, two sensors per shaft and rigid alignment Current selection: four sensors Vishay TCST1103 family Another bare transmissive option with a documented mechanical package Mechanical fit and optical response require comparison with the actual disk Alternative if mounting favors this package Custom reflective optical arrangement Could read a patterned surface without placing a disk inside a fork Depends on reflectance, ambient light and sensor standoff; needs new optical characterization Architecture alternative; specific part unselected

The TCST2103 keeps the design based on ordinary motors and gives each shaft an A/B pair. The sensor choice is conditional on disk and bracket fit. A built-in encoder motor would simplify mounting but would change the project's selected approach and needs team approval.

docs.title: Analog amplification — individual subsystem
docs.text:
Candidate Advantages Limitations Decision MCP6004 Four amplifier channels in one IC; rail-to-rail input/output family; 1 MHz class Current gain drives high inputs into saturation; recovery must be tested Current selection: U2, nominal gain 1.5 MCP6024 Quad rail-to-rail family with 10 MHz bandwidth More bandwidth may increase sensitivity to noise; power/package review needed Alternative if measured edge response requires it Two dual amplifiers Splits channels across two packages for placement flexibility Larger BOM and layout; exact device and supply compatibility unselected Architecture alternative

Each channel uses a 10 kΩ feedback resistor and 20 kΩ resistor to ground: 1 + 10k/20k = 1.5. The 4.7 kΩ / 1 nF network has a nominal pole near 33.9 kHz and a time constant of 4.7 µs. Phototransistor impedance changes the actual response. Optical contrast, amplifier rail behavior and pulse timing require measurement before these values can be accepted.

docs.title: Digital edge conditioning — individual subsystem
docs.text:
Candidate Advantages Limitations Decision SN74HC14 Six Schmitt inverter gates; four are sufficient for the encoder signals Thresholds and dynamic supply current must be checked at operating voltage and edge rate Current selection: SN74HC14N / U3 CD40106B Six Schmitt inverter gates; broad supply range Timing and thresholds differ; cannot substitute without checking the pulse rate Alternative PIC input conditioning only Fewer external components Relies on PIC input behavior and software; removes the explicit external Schmitt stage Architecture alternative requiring redesign

The four used HC14 gates provide consistent edge conditioning. Unused inputs are tied to a defined level in the schematic. Both channels of each quadrature pair are inverted, so firmware must establish the actual forward direction during calibration.

docs.title: Regulation and power source
docs.text:
Regulator option Advantages Limitations Decision ST L78 / L7805ACV Simple local 5 V rail; familiar through-hole package; matches Revision B Linear dissipation rises with input voltage; heatsink and load must be verified Current schematic selection ST L4940V5 Lower dropout can help when input headroom is limited At the same input/output/current, linear heat remains similar; stability and pinout need review Alternative, not a drop-in approval

The team PRD specifies an individual 9 V wall adapter; Revision B labels its jack 9–12 V. A current-limited bench supply is suitable for development. A final adapter model, plug dimensions, current rating and procurement price have not been selected. A battery option adds runtime, charging and discharge considerations without a current project need. The power budget explains why 9 V is thermally preferable to 12 V for the same load.

docs.title: PIC pins and MCC configuration plan
docs.text:
This is the configuration to implement and verify in MCC, derived from the schematic's Nano connector labels. No completed MCC project or screenshot is available in the reviewed files. Edge numbers below refer to the Nano board, not the MCU package pins.

Signal PIC pin Nano edge Planned configuration E1A_DIG RB0 46 Digital input; interrupt-on-change candidate E1B_DIG RB1 10 Digital input; interrupt-on-change candidate E2A_DIG RB2 9 Digital input; interrupt-on-change candidate E2B_DIG RB3 47 Digital input; interrupt-on-change candidate MCU_TX → JP1 → ENC_TX RC6 13 UART TX via peripheral pin select; final UART instance and baud pending ENC_RX RC7 19 UART RX via peripheral pin select; team protocol pending DEBUG_LED RA3 16 Digital output; choose initial low state DEBUG_BTN RA4 17 Digital input; stable-state firmware debounce Spare GPIO RA0 / RA1 43 / 44 Reserved; do not assign conflicting peripherals External +5 V VTG 51 Verify Nano external-power procedure; VOFF edge 55 tied to ground

Disable analog functions on digital signals, configure the selected clock and timing source, initialize quadrature state before enabling interrupts, and verify the worst-case interrupt rate. A periodic timer and an atomic count snapshot can support speed reporting. UART framing, signed count width, update period and fault handling remain firmware design decisions.

docs.title: Schematic Design
docs.text:
Revision B implements four optical channels for two motors, local 5 V regulation, a PIC18F57Q43 Nano, debug I/O and the proposed serial interface to the main board. The full schematic is embedded below; select the image to zoom, or open the PDF to inspect small labels.

Figure 2. Revision B, reviewed October 27, 2026 in KiCad 10.0.7.

High-resolution schematic PDF Complete KiCad project ZIP ERC report JSON Engineering review notes

docs.title: 1. Protected local power
docs.text:
J1 takes a center-positive 9–12 V source. F1 feeds VIN_FUSED, and the L7805ACV generates +5 V. Input/output capacitors and local decoupling support the regulator and ICs; the green power LED indicates that the rail is present. Test points expose VIN_FUSED, +5 V and ground. Regulator thermal performance must be verified using the power budget.

The Nano is represented as a passive connector: +5 V enters VTG edge 51 and VOFF edge 55 is grounded, following the external-power approach documented in the Nano user guide. VBUS edge 56 is not connected in this design. Check board orientation and the guide before connecting external power and USB.

docs.title: 2. Optical current to analog voltage
docs.text: Four off-board TCST2103 sensors monitor the two disks. Each emitter uses a 220 Ω series resistor, giving approximately (5 − 1.25) / 220 = 17 mA under the stated nominal forward-drop assumption. The phototransistor collector works with a 4.7 kΩ pull-up and a 1 nF capacitor. TP4–TP7 expose the raw channels for blocked/unblocked testing.

docs.title: 3. Amplification and digital edges
docs.text: U2 is a quad MCP6004. Each non-inverting stage has nominal gain 1.5; a high raw signal can drive its output into positive saturation. That behavior makes saturation recovery, rail levels and pulse width key bench tests. The SN74HC14 then applies Schmitt hysteresis and inversion before RB0–RB3 receive the signals. The filter's nominal 33.9 kHz pole is a calculation, not a demonstrated operating-rate limit.

docs.title: 4. Counting and reporting
docs.text: The PIC's proposed firmware tracks transitions in each A/B pair and reports counts and timing to the main board. RC6 TX passes through JP1 to J6; removing JP1 isolates the transmit path. RC7 receives ENC_RX. The proposed connection is 5 V logic UART, not RS-232 voltage levels. Shared multidriver operation has not been approved; the team must resolve addressing/topology and avoid output contention.

docs.title: 5. Debug and serviceability
docs.text: RA3 drives the yellow debug LED. RA4 reads SW1 with R19 and C11; firmware debounce remains necessary. RA0/RA1 are available at J7. Labeled connectors, channel test points and the TX jumper support independent bring-up of the power, sensing and communication stages.

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text:
This preliminary encoder-board planning estimate accounts for the four emitters, PIC board, analog/logic ICs and support loads, then adds the required 25% margin. Motors are powered on the motor-driver subsystem and are excluded from this local rail.

Estimate, not a verified maximum-current budget

The Nano, amplifier and logic entries include explicitly labeled planning allowances. They are not measured results or datasheet absolute maxima. A final course-template budget requires verified worst-case operating currents, the exact adapter and thermal measurements. Absolute maximum ratings are stress limits and should not be used as intended operating points.

docs.title: A · Loads on the +5 V rail
docs.text: Load Quantity Unit current (mA) Total (mA) Basis Nano board + MCU 1 100.00 100.00 Planning allowance; actual firmware/debugger load unmeasured TCST2103 emitters 4 17.05 68.18 Calculated nominal, 220 ohm / 1.25 V assumed LED drop Collector pull-ups 4 1.06 4.26 All four raw nodes low; conservative pull-up bound MCP6004 + feedback 1 2.00 2.00 Planning allowance including output/feedback loading SN74HC14 1 5.00 5.00 Planning allowance; depends on input edges and frequency Power + debug LEDs 2 3.00 6.00 Planning allowance, 1k series resistors Debug pull-up 1 0.50 0.50 Button held low, 10k at 5 V

docs.title: B · Rail demand and margin
docs.text:
Result Planning estimate Sum of local +5 V loads 185.94 mA Safety margin 25% +5 V design-current estimate with margin 232.42 mA Output power at the margin load 1.162 W

The emitters alone account for about 68 mA under the nominal forward-drop assumption. Measure blocked/unblocked sensor currents and the running Nano board to replace the allowances. Current uncertainty and regulator heating matter more than the regulator's headline current rating.

docs.title: C · Regulator and thermal check
docs.text:
The schematic uses L7805ACV. Ignoring regulator ground current, P_loss = (V_in − 5 V) × I_out.

Input Dissipation at 232.42 mA Ideal linear conversion efficiency 9 V 0.930 W 55.6% 12 V 1.627 W 41.7%

Regulator ground current adds input demand and dissipation. A heatsink/thermal design cannot be accepted from these numbers alone: check the actual package's junction-to-ambient or heatsink path, ambient temperature, maximum junction temperature and mounting. At the earlier review example of 250 mA, 12 V input produces approximately 1.75 W before ground-current loss.

docs.title: D · External source
docs.text:
The team PRD specifies a 9 V wall adapter, while the schematic allows 9–12 V at J1. A particular adapter is still unselected. Its usable continuous current must exceed the margin load plus regulator ground current, with appropriate polarity and connector fit. Until its rated output and regulator current are verified, remaining source capacity is unavailable. Start bring-up with a current-limited bench supply.

The drawn 500 mA fuse does not establish a safe supply rating or guaranteed semiconductor protection. Check the time-current characteristic, inrush, wiring and regulator thermal limits before accepting it.

docs.title: E · Battery runtime
docs.text: Not applicable to the current wall-powered concept. If a battery is selected later, add usable capacity, discharge limits, conversion loss and runtime at the verified load.

docs.title: Reusable calculation
docs.text:
Editable power-budget workbook Machine-readable inputs

The workbook follows sections A–E and exposes the assumptions. It is a working planning model; final supplier and measurement data must replace the marked allowances before claiming a completed worst-case course budget.

docs.title: Bench verification sequence
docs.text:
1. Inspect connector orientation and continuity with power disconnected. Confirm fuse, regulator pins and the Nano external-power wiring.
  2. Power the disconnected logic board from a current-limited supply; measure VIN_FUSED and +5 V, then check full-load temperature with the complete assembly.
  3. Block and unblock each optical sensor. Probe TP4â€“TP7, U2 outputs and HC14 outputs for voltage levels, noise and saturation recovery.
  4. Rotate each disk in both directions. Check A/B phase order, known counts per revolution and the highest required edge rate.
  5. Implement firmware counting, a home/reference procedure and stable-state button debounce; verify interrupt loading and count snapshot integrity.
  6. Agree the final serial link and connect one board at a time. Test TX isolation, framing, stale-data behavior and power-off conditions.
